transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-06-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions), John Rivera (Kestrel Eng Lead), Priya Nair (Kestrel PM), Ellen Zhao (Kestrel SRE)

Summary:
Quick scoping to align on POC success criteria for latency and throughput SLOs, pick TTFT vs TPOT targets, define measurement plan and scheduling pilot runs. Agreed to run warm/cold cache benchmarks, 10k-sample p95/p99 analysis, and provide test harness. Action items and dates captured below.

Topics:
- TTFT vs TPOT semantics and tradeoffs
- Target p95/p99 values for chat vs embed workloads
- Measurement plan: synthetic vs replay, sample sizes, warm vs cold cache
- Benchmark tooling, configs, and scheduling
- Pilot node sizing and A/B conditions

Transcript:
[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call — I'm Alicia from Redwood, Marco SE, Samir solutions. John, Priya, Ellen, you there?
[00:12] John: Yep, hi all. John here. Sorry, running a bit behind, coffee in hand.
[00:16] Priya: Priya joining.
[00:19] Ellen: Ellen, SRE.
[00:22] Marco: Awesome. Goal for today, align on SLOs for the POC — specifically TTFT versus TPOT, p95/p99 targets, and how we'll measure them. I'll start with how we usually define both, but we want to hear Kestrel's success criteria first.
[00:38] John: Great. Our immediate worry is user-facing chat latency. We need a consistent experience for customers on mobile. Historically our threshold for first-response perceived latency is around 300ms — anything over that feels laggy. But at scale we can't pay for one-off latency optimizations without seeing tradeoffs in throughput and cost.
[00:56] Alicia: Makes sense. For clarity: TTFT = time to first token (server processing + first token emit), TPOT = time per token (steady-state per-token latency). The engineering tradeoff is you can tune for TTFT with smaller contexts or different batching config which may increase per-token cost, whereas optimizing TPOT often involves larger batch sizes and kernel choices — slightly higher TTFT but lower overall token cost.
[01:20] Priya: So when customers say "fast", they usually mean TTFT, right? First byte experienced by the client. But for long responses TPOT matters because total completion time is TTFT + tokens*TPOT.
[01:33] Marco: Exactly.
[01:35] Samir: Also we have to call out library effects — quantization or flash-attn kernels will change TPOT but TTFT might spike on cold KV-caches.
[01:45] John: We definitely care about both. If we set TTFT at 200ms p95 and TPOT at 15ms p95, we can model completion times for our 80th-percentile prompt length of ~90 tokens. That gives us TTFT + 90*15ms = 200 + 1350 = 1.55s which fits our UX target.
[02:10] Ellen: Is 15ms per token realistic for the models we plan to use? We're looking to use the 7B family quantized to int8 on A100s for the pilot.
[02:21] Marco: On A100 with good kernel paths and batching, 12-18ms/token is realistic at moderate concurrency. But p99 tails will be worse — maybe 30-40ms/token if you include noisy neighbors and cold cache scenarios. That's why we propose separate p95 and p99 targets and a fallback policy.
[02:40] Priya: Can you explain fallback policy? We have to keep the chat online even if tails blow up.
[02:45] Alicia: Sure — Redwood supports routing rules: if latency spikes above the p99 threshold we can automatically fallback to a higher-capacity variant or a hosted lower-cost model. For the POC we'll define an automatic failover to a dedicated reserved pool or to a smaller quantized model depending on the scenario.
[02:59] John: OK. So for the POC acceptance, we want two buckets: interactive SLO for TTFT and throughput-compute SLO for TPOT. Proposed starting targets from Redwood?
[03:12] Marco: For an interactive chat baseline on the 7B quantized model, we'd propose TTFT p95 <= 220ms, TTFT p99 <= 420ms. TPOT p95 <= 16ms/token, TPOT p99 <= 36ms/token. Those are initial, we can tighten after the first run. For embeddings/async workloads we set TPOT p95 <= 25ms and p99 <= 60ms since batch sizes differ.
[03:38] Priya: Those numbers are helpful. Can we also capture cold-cache behavior? Many of our requests are first-time prompt variants.
[03:46] Marco: Yes — measurement plan includes separate cold-start run where we clear KV cache between each request and measure TTFT distribution; warm-run retains cache. We'll report both.
[03:56] John: Regarding measurement methodology, what sample sizes do you recommend? We want statistical confidence at p99.
[04:03] Marco: For p99 stability we aim for at least 5k-10k measured requests per condition. So, e.g., 10k warm requests, 10k cold requests, and a minimum 30-minute sustained run at target QPS to observe tail behavior. We'll do three iterations to check variance.
[04:20] Ellen: How do you emulate our traffic? We have a mix of short and long responses — distribution skewed right.
[04:27] Marco: We recommend a replay of a recent traffic trace that captures the prompt length distribution; if you can't share traces we can use a synthetic traffic profile matching your percentile lengths: p50=45 tokens, p80=90, p95=180, with a small set of corner cases >512 tokens.
[04:42] Priya: John, can you share the 2-week traffic trace scrubbed of PII?
[04:47] John: I can. I'll ask SRE for an anonymized trace. Expect that by Friday.
[04:52] Alicia: Great. Tooling — we typically provide a harness based on Locust + custom collectors; we can also run native Redwood benchmarker which instruments TTFT/TPOT with per-token timestamps. We'll send the harness and a sample config.
[05:06] Samir: Quick note: when we instrument per-token timing we sometimes see measurement overhead. We'll subtract known probe latency and publish raw and adjusted numbers so you can verify.
[05:16] Ellen: For the pilot, what's the suggested node footprint? We want to reserve a realistic dedicated pool.
[05:21] Marco: Based on your QPS target (you mentioned 40 QPS peak?), for 7B quantized on A100, rough sizing is: 3 dedicated GPUs for baseline (sustained 40 QPS with moderate batching) with autoscale to 6 GPUs for bursts. We'll draft a sizing calc with assumptions.
[05:38] John: We have traffic spikes up to 120 QPS in marketing campaigns — need burst headroom.
[05:44] Marco: Then plan on a 6 GPU baseline for the pilot with ability to add 4 more for bursts. For the pilot we'll simulate those spikes in a separate stress test to validate autoscale and fallback rules.
[05:54] Priya: On measurement windows, do we capture only successful responses or include errors/timeouts in the SLO?
[06:00] Alicia: SLO composition: we recommended including successful responses only for raw latency SLOs but also track error rates separately as an availability metric — e.g., 99.9% success rate over the pilot, with latency SLO applied to successful responses. We'll also flag timeouts as failures for the customer's UX SLA.
[06:17] John: Makes sense.
[06:20] Marco: A couple of gotchas — quantized models can have jitter on first token if caches aren't primed; so we also measure a "primed cold" scenario where we run a single priming request per model instance before measuring.
[06:33] Samir: For reproducibility we'll freeze model hash/version, tokenizer version, and CUDA/cuDNN stack during runs and record env details in the benchmark results.
[06:44] Priya: On SLO pass/fail criteria: do we require both p95 and p99 to pass or can we have graduated acceptance? We need to roll to prod progressively.
[06:53] Marco: We usually define a primary target (p95) for go/no-go and a secondary acceptance band (p99) for graduation. Proposal: p95 targets must meet for the pilot to be considered successful; p99 must be within 1.5x of target with an action plan to remediate.
[07:06] John: That seems reasonable.
[07:09] Marco: We'll also add cost per 1M tokens estimate for each config so you can trade-off economics vs latency.
[07:16] Alicia: Next steps — I'll send the pricing + SOC2 snapshot, Marco will send the harness and detailed test plan. Can we tentatively start pilot runs week of 6/29?
[07:25] Priya: That works for our timeline — Q3 feature launch dependent on pilot success so we need results by mid-July ideally.
[07:33] John: We'll aim to prioritize the traffic trace and 1k sample prompts.
[07:36] Ellen: And I'll validate infra access for a private pool test.
[07:39] Samir: Anything else on acceptance criteria? We should formalize the SLO doc with numeric targets and measurement traces.
[07:45] Priya: Yes, a short acceptance doc would be great.
[07:47] Alicia: Noted. We'll produce a one-page acceptance matrix: TTFT p95/p99, TPOT p95/p99, error rate threshold, sample sizes, and warm vs cold test definitions. We'll attach the harness and the config.
[07:59] Marco: Any competitor concerns?
[08:01] John: We ran a quick benchmark with one of the public providers — tail latency was worse there; the reason we talked to Redwood is for predictable tails and control over private footprint.
[08:11] Alicia: OK thanks. We'll include comparisons where useful but focus on baseline.
[08:15] Priya: Also include test notes about caching strategy: prefix caching vs KV-cache eviction policy, which matters a lot for chat.
[08:24] Marco: Good call.
[08:27] John: One last question — how do we record per-token timings from the client side? We have mobile SDKs where we wouldn't have per-token timestamps.
[08:36] Marco: For mobile you can measure time-to-first-byte at the SDK and total completion time as a black-box. We'll correlate server-side per-token telemetry with client-side RUM for full picture.
[08:45] Ellen: Alright. If no other questions we'll wrap.
[08:48] Priya: Thanks all.
[08:50] Alicia: Thank you, we'll follow up with notes and the deliverables.

Appendix - Quick measurement plan (high level):
1) Recreate traffic profile (replay or synthetic) matching token length distribution
2) Run cold-run suite (clear cache each request) 10k samples
3) Run warm-run suite 10k samples, sustained 30m at target QPS
4) Spike tests to 3x baseline for autoscale/fallback validation
5) Repeat 3 iterations and report p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT plus error rates
6) Publish environment hashes, raw logs, and cost estimate per 1M tokens
